extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in literary theory, drama, and Aristotle's Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for composing and analysing dramatic poetry (especially tragedy) according to Aristotle's Poetics, including the canonical elements of tragedy and what makes a plot/character effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is 'a representation of a serious, complete action that has magnitude, in embellished speech, with each of its elements [used] separately in the [various] parts [of the play] and [represented] by people acting and not by narration, accomplished using pity and terror the catharsis of such emotions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key parts of the definition: seriousness, completeness, magnitude, embellished speech (rhythm and melody), action represented by actors (not narration), and the production of pity and fear leading to catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: The six parts/elements of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's constituent parts of tragedy: Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), Thought (dianoia), Diction (lexis), Melody (melos), and Spectacle (opsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each element has a distinct evaluative role (plot is primary). The chorus should be treated as an actoral element contributing to melody and unity. Spectacle is considered the least artistic and least connected with the poet's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (mythos) – organization of incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot refers to the 'organization of incidents' and should imitate an action that evokes pity and fear; plots involve change of fortune (good to bad or bad to good), and complex plots include reversals (peripeteia) and recognitions (anagnorisis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good plots: (a) evoke pity and fear; (b) have logical causal sequence where actions follow from preceding events and character; (c) favor complex plots with reversal and recognition; (d) the most tragic plot often pushes a good character toward undeserved misfortune because of a mistake (hamartia); (e) violent situations between friends or family are especially tragic; (f) actions should be plausible consequences so surprises feel necessary after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos) – moral and psychological fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' moral qualities and choices reveal actions that excite pity and fear; in a perfect tragedy, character supports plot so that motivations and traits connect causes and effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main character should be: good (not morally extreme), appropriate (e.g., wisdom corresponding to age/position), realistic, and consistent. Sudden unexplained changes ('consistently inconsistent') should be explained or flagged as a trait; characters must act according to the Law of Probability and Necessity (internal consistency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (error/miscalculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic plots frequently revolve around a mistake (hamartia) that causes the hero's downfall; such an error often makes the misfortune seem undeserved and thus arouses pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamartia is not merely moral flaw but a mistake or miscalculation; plots where a good character is led to undeserved misfortune by error are especially tragic and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal) and Anagnorisis (recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis) are crucial components of complex plots: peripeteia is a sudden change of fortune and anagnorisis is a change from ignorance to knowledge about a person or situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination of reversal and recognition is highly effective at producing pity and fear; Aristotle judges certain orders (e.g., ignorance followed by discovery) as particularly satisfying, though there are debates about which arrangement is most tragic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis and tragic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should produce 'tragic pleasure' by effecting the proper catharsis (purgation/clarification/purification) of pity and fear in the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy's concentrated effect—achieved through unity and compressed time—makes it more pleasurable than epic for producing catharsis; the dramatic arrangement should aim to arouse and then release these emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, completeness, and magnitude of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The play must present a complete and whole action of a certain magnitude (suitable scope/importance) and maintain unity so that constituent elements are bound by probability and necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poet should visualize all scenes, incorporate complication and dénouement, and combine elements so the plot is unified rather than a plurality of disconnected actions (the epic is criticized for plurality). Magnitude implies appropriate scale so the action feels complete and significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) – ideas and reasoning expressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought refers to the themes and spoken reasoning of characters; the reasoning should explicate characters or background and express meaningful ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought is manifested through what characters say and do; playwrights should express reasoning through characters' speech so ideas are integrated with action and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) – quality and appropriateness of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the quality of speech or language in tragedy; speeches should reflect character and express the meaning of the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lexis should be fitted to characters' moral and social qualities; diction contributes to the believability of character and to the conveyance of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody (melos) and the role of chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (often music-dance) is an integral material of poetic composition; the Chorus should be written as one of the actors and contribute to the unity and pleasure of the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melos includes music, dance, and correlated movement; chorus must take part in action and strengthen unity rather than being a mere ornamental addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis) – visual apparatus and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle refers to the visual elements of the play (sets, costumes, props); Aristotle calls spectacle the 'least artistic' element and 'least connected with the work of the poet (playwright)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle can enhance a production but should not substitute for good plot, character, or acting; beautiful visuals cannot make up for a bad story or poor performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter/Means of mimesis (language, rhythm, melody) and methods of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes poetic 'matter' as language, rhythm, and melody. Methods of imitation vary: narration, mixed narration and direct speech (Homeric), or direct speech (actors) as in tragedy and comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The selection of means (e.g., use of chorus, song, or purely verbal narrative) affects genre and effectiveness; tragic drama uses direct speech/actors rather than narrator, and may integrate music and dance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects/agents and genre differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle differentiates genres by the kinds of human characters: tragedy treats serious, important, and virtuous people; comedy treats less virtuous people and human foibles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing the appropriate social and moral status of characters is part of genre construction (tripartite division: superior, inferior, or equal to the audience). The nature of agents should match genre expectations to produce the intended emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs history – universals and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (including tragedy) concerns what might occur and approximates knowledge of universals; history records particulars marked by contingency and chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should craft plots according to logical probability and necessity to convey universal truths, rather than merely recounting particular past events; this makes poetic narrative more philosophical in Aristotle's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructional advice for the poet/playwright
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical guidance: the poet should visualize all scenes, incorporate complication and dénouement within the story, combine all elements of tragedy, and express thought through characters' words and actions while attending to diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural prescriptions emphasize planning (visualization), structural coherence (complication/dénouement), integration of elements (plot, character, diction, melody), and expression of theme through action rather than exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative standard: tragedy's superiority to epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle argues tragedy is artistically superior to epic because it contains what epic has yet achieves a more concentrated and pleasurable effect due to unity and compressed time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating genre effectiveness, consider unity, concentration of effect, and the ability to produce catharsis—tragedy is favored on these grounds despite epics' broader material.
